approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Rock metrics are a useful capture layer for dashboard history because they can run off-hours, store repeatable values, and support later visualization without repeatedly recalculating expensive operational queries.

notes: Read-only SQL verified Metric, MetricValue, and Schedule columns that support scheduled metric capture and later dashboard visualization.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: For dashboard speed, expensive journey analytics can be calculated into a persisted dataset on a schedule rather than recalculating all historical engagement data on each page load.

notes: Read-only SQL verified PersistedDataset exists with refresh interval, schedule, result data, cache, Lava command, and build script columns.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: This Data Analytics Hub walkthrough describes a Rock-based journey engagement dashboard that combines content-channel journey definitions, group/member participation, group member attendance, campus filters, persisted datasets, and Lava chart shortcodes to help ministry teams evaluate engagement and improve content strategy.

External BI tools become more useful when questions require complex modeling, multiple source systems, high-level KPI reporting, or visualization patterns that are difficult to keep performant inside Rock alone.
Migration plans should identify which system is the trusted source of truth for person, contribution, check-in, and event data before expanding to optional ministry workflows.

source_refs.title: Episode 111: Special Edition with Tim Dear

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Contributor-authored KB material should aim for accessible explanations that church staff can use, not only developer-oriented technical detail.

source_refs.title: Episode 91: Special Edition with Cullen McCoy

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: This RockCast profile adds public-safe context for check-in implementation work: real deployments can require long troubleshooting cycles, church-specific process mapping, and low-level label-printing knowledge such as ZPL. It is useful routing evidence for check-in, implementation, and developer troubleshooting topics.

For member surveys, public or shared results should avoid direct personal identifiers and return church-specific data in aggregated form so teams learn from patterns without turning the study into a person-level accountability list.

This Data Analytics Hub panel gives a practical decision frame for Rock-native reporting versus external BI tools. The panel favors starting with Rock metrics, Data Views, Lava, Dynamic Data, and embedded pages for operational or person-actionable workflows, while using BI tools for complex joins, third-party sources, leadership KPIs, and broader analytical exploration.
A phased Rock launch can prioritize write-back or money-moving surfaces first, then add ministry areas after staff have a stable foundation.

source_refs.title: Episode 111: Special Edition with Tim Dear

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: This RockCast implementation story adds public-safe migration guidance. Pine Lake described moving quickly but deliberately by making Rock the source of truth first for database-updating surfaces such as contributions, check-in, and paid/basic events, then phasing additional ministry areas after the foundation was live.

source_refs.title: Episode 111: Special Edition with Tim Dear

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Caching and distributed-cache discussion should be used as architecture context only; concrete performance guidance needs current Rock documentation, live configuration, and measured behavior.

source_refs.title: Episode 33: Rock 7.3 and New RX2018 Tracks

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Caching and cache clearing are developer-support surfaces because content changes may not appear immediately unless the right cache path is refreshed.

Before building custom cleanup processes, review Rock's built-in data automation options such as profile activation/inactivation rules, adult-child family movement, and gender classification thresholds.

This Data Analytics Hub presentation describes a church analytics architecture that separates reporting models from operational Rock data, uses SQL/dbt-style modeling to simplify complex Rock tables, and presents dashboards as decision tools rather than decorative scoreboards. It emphasizes simple visualizations, mission-aligned measures, and pre/post measurement when evaluating ministry initiatives.

Data volunteers can help with duplicate and cleanup queues, but they need training, review time, and bounded scope; adding more volunteers does not scale if every merge decision still requires staff judgment.
Rock-native tools are a strong first option for simpler dashboards, operational reports, and person-actionable workflows because they keep users close to the ministry record and workflow context.

When collecting cross-church survey data, keep the question set consistent across participating churches, test communications and survey flow, and define in advance what data will be returned to each partner.
Rock documentation and Rock U material should be treated as official training sources that explain both feature behavior and intended use.

source_refs.title: Episode 91: Special Edition with Cullen McCoy

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Publishing a ministry dashboard can change behavior when it exposes underused content or completion gaps; teams can then adjust marketing, launch timing, content length, and follow-up strategy based on observed engagement.

Journey reporting may need to join content-channel items, generated groups, group members, notes/comments, and attendance-style completion events because the ministry experience spans both content and group participation models.

Campus dashboards should help leaders compare current year-to-date values against both goals and prior-year context, while leaving deeper campus-specific measures available without crowding the organization-wide dashboard.
A mature reporting suite can separate executive dashboards, campus or ministry dashboards, and functional operational dashboards so each audience sees the level of detail needed for its decisions.

Functional dashboards such as connection-request views may justify live database connections when leaders need up-to-date queues, while slower-changing attendance or giving dashboards can usually use scheduled refreshes.

When AI summaries are generated from person-profile data, the review should include data minimization, avoidance of direct identifiers, privacy-policy alignment, and vendor assurances about model training.

A practical cleanup program should separate low-effort automations from medium-effort reports and high-effort duplicate decisions, so staff and volunteers spend human review time on records that require judgment.
When embedding Power BI or similar reports in Rock, pair report pages with appropriate Rock security roles and licensing checks so only authorized, licensed users can access the embedded dashboards.

notes: Read-only SQL verified report pages/blocks and Auth rows exist for Rock-side security review of embedded BI surfaces.
This does not verify external BI licensing.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Entity Framework is an important developer-track topic for understanding how Rock code works with data models and should be routed with developer resources.

Rock plugin and theme packaging guidance frames the Rock Shop as the distribution path for community extensions, so plugin work should include packaging, review, and uninstall behavior rather than only local code changes.
Check-in support often reaches into label-printer details such as ZPL, so label issues should be routed to both check-in behavior and printer/template implementation context.

This Digital Strategy Hub presentation provides public-safe guidance for churches evaluating AI. It frames AI as a fast-moving tool category that can assist ministry work, but requires clear use cases, privacy boundaries, staff training, review expectations, and model/vendor awareness before it is connected to Rock data or public-facing experiences.
AI should be introduced around concrete ministry workflows and reviewable outputs, not as a broad replacement for staff judgment.

Episode 202 adds public-safe operational context for Rock release awareness, community-shaped priorities, AI-assisted group matching, and documentation currency; concrete implementation guidance remains tied to official docs, release notes, source code, or live-instance verification.

source_refs.title: Rock's Future Anchored in Vision | Ep 202

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Historical Rock data should be used selectively: event, finance, and reliable attendance history are often safer than demographic or group-member history, which may reflect current-state changes rather than past reality.

This RockCast profile adds public-safe context for several developer-facing Rock surfaces: core UI/UX work, cache clearing, Wi-Fi presence, registration changes, and Entity Framework education. It is useful as routing evidence for developer troubleshooting and for treating registration, caching, and presence features as implementation areas with deeper internals.

For ministry efforts with subjective outcomes, teams can still define desired outcomes before launch and compare before/after measurements to learn whether the effort changed behavior, sentiment, or engagement.
Data analytics meetups can help churches compare dashboards, process designs, and BI-tool choices against real ministry use cases instead of treating reporting as an isolated technical task.

Episode 33 adds public-safe operational context for major-release validation, non-admin test coverage, family pre-registration roadmap awareness, and caching architecture; implementation claims should be checked against current official sources and live configuration.

source_refs.title: Episode 33: Rock 7.3 and New RX2018 Tracks

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Volunteer scheduling was framed as a major roadmap item, so serving and group-scheduling guides should route scheduling questions through both release history and current model/feature documentation.

source_refs.title: Episode 40: v8 and more team updates

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Dashboards should answer specific, decision-oriented questions; vague requests such as broad small-group performance should be split into narrower measures that a ministry leader can act on.

For AI-assisted group finding, implementation work needs church-specific matching rules: which group types are findable, which attributes describe affinity, and what boundaries keep the assistant away from inappropriate targets such as security roles.

source_refs.title: Rock's Future Anchored in Vision | Ep 202

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: A reporting layer can simplify Rock's operational schema for analysts by modeling ministry concepts into reporting-friendly tables or views while leaving source data unchanged.

This RockCast update is useful public roadmap context: v8 was discussed as moving toward alpha testing, v9 was framed around volunteer scheduling, and Wi-Fi presence was described as an integration that maps campus Wi-Fi signals into Rock attendance-style insight. The episode also highlights privacy and data-ownership concerns when external services participate in presence tracking.

source_refs.title: Episode 40: v8 and more team updates

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Large Rock releases can carry accumulated change and post-release fixes, so upgrade planning should distinguish major-version validation from routine patch-release validation and verify current release notes before action.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: This RockCast profile adds public-safe context for how official Rock documentation and Rock U videos are positioned: they are intended to keep pace with product changes, explain how features should be used, and remain accessible to non-developer church staff. This is useful for contributor guidance and source-priority decisions.

source_refs.title: Episode 91: Special Edition with Cullen McCoy

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: For Rock dashboards, shape complex reporting data in SQL or a prepared query layer and use Lava primarily for display so later maintenance does not require tracing business logic across both SQL and presentation code.
Small-group matching research should start with a clear ministry question and consistent survey design so responses can support future matching improvements rather than one-off local reports.
Release-roadmap podcast material is useful as historical context but should not override current release notes when agents answer version-specific questions.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: This Data Analytics Hub session adds public-safe guidance for group-matching research and external analytics tooling. It frames small-group matching as a data problem involving consistent survey design, privacy boundaries, aggregated results, and cross-church analysis, then shows how Rock analytics-enabled tables and external BI tools can support engagement snapshots and richer dashboard views.

Executive dashboards work better when they expose a small set of organization-wide goals with clear current values, goal values, and status indicators instead of hiding many rolled-up metrics behind ambiguous scores.

Rock's analytics-enabled tables can be used as a snapshot layer for engagement-style metrics, allowing external reporting tools to query daily counts or trends without repeatedly reconstructing every operational detail.

notes: Read-only SQL verified metric, metric value, DataView persistence, and PersistedDataset surfaces that can support snapshot-style analytics tables and daily trend reporting.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: After go-live, teams should shift from launch pressure to quality requirements, sprint planning, and intentionally redesigned ministry processes.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Family pre-registration was discussed as roadmap and consulting context for website or kiosk entry points; treat it as a prompt to verify the current block, check-in, and kiosk capabilities before designing an intake flow.

source_refs.title: Episode 33: Rock 7.3 and New RX2018 Tracks

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: This Data Analytics Hub presentation gives public-safe operational guidance for Rock data quality programs: use built-in automation where possible, prioritize a small number of high-value data defects, move actionable cleanup reports into Rock, train a bounded volunteer team, and connect data quality work to ministry outcomes such as check-in, communication, and leadership reporting.

This Data Analytics Hub session adds public-safe dashboard-design guidance for Rock reporting work: start with actionable questions, keep charts tied to decisions, avoid dashboards when a KPI or existing page element is enough, and treat historical Rock data differently depending on whether the source records are stable enough for comparison.
Alpha and beta testing should include non-administrator staff personas, because admin-only testing can hide authorization and role-specific defects that normal staff encounter.

source_refs.title: Episode 33: Rock 7.3 and New RX2018 Tracks

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Migration work can expose single-person operational knowledge, making documentation and shared process ownership part of the implementation plan.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Use the episode as release-awareness context: podcast release discussion can flag security updates, alpha/beta status, and future model-changing work, but upgrade guidance must still be verified against official release notes and the local Rock version.

source_refs.title: Rock's Future Anchored in Vision | Ep 202

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Attendance-flow analysis can move beyond aggregate weekend counts by classifying engagement patterns, prioritizing follow-up lists, and creating Rock connection requests for campus teams.

The Data Analytics Hub launch frames community analytics as a shared practice space where churches compare dashboards, ministry processes, BI tooling, and Rock-based reporting patterns. The session also includes a Life.Church attendance-flow case study that uses Rock attendance and connection data to prioritize pastoral follow-up while treating AI profile summaries and privacy controls as governance concerns.

Documentation changes should be planned as part of UI and release work; major UI changes can create downstream screenshot and article-refresh work that must be tracked before public guidance is treated as current.

source_refs.title: Rock's Future Anchored in Vision | Ep 202

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: This RockCast implementation story is useful public-safe guidance for migrations and platform configuration. Red Rocks described discovery as a chance to bring ministries together, expose informal processes, reduce spreadsheet-heavy work, and ask whether Rock should automate or improve a process rather than simply recreate the previous system.

source_refs.title: Episode 84: Special Edition with Red Rocks

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: A Rock Check-in implementation can involve process mapping and extended troubleshooting, not only enabling the check-in feature.

A journey dashboard can define completion as finishing every day in a journey, then use group member attendance and participation records to compare completion across solo, group, spouse, campus, demographic, and journey-category dimensions.
A Rock discovery process should include ministry stakeholders early because it can reveal workflows, data handoffs, and manual spreadsheet work that staff may not have formalized.

source_refs.title: Episode 84: Special Edition with Red Rocks

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: AI governance should include staff training, data-minimization rules, and a review path before AI-generated content or data summaries influence public communication or pastoral action.
Effective dashboards should communicate a clear story, focus attention on decisions, and avoid overloading leaders with more measures than they can act on.
Because AI model capabilities and vendor terms change quickly, churches should document which tools are approved and what data classes may be used with each one.
When migrating to Rock, teams should ask why a process exists and whether it should be automated or redesigned instead of recreating every legacy step.

source_refs.title: Episode 84: Special Edition with Red Rocks

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Community feedback channels such as Rocket Chat, calls, church visits, and conferences can explain why areas like Connections rise in priority, but agents should treat that as roadmap context rather than proof that a feature is present in a given instance.

source_refs.title: Rock's Future Anchored in Vision | Ep 202

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Wi-Fi presence connects campus network signals to person attendance-style insight, which makes data ownership, vendor behavior, and privacy review part of the implementation guidance.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: External BI tools can combine Rock tables, query outputs, spreadsheets, and other data sources into one view, but teams should choose the approach based on resources, expertise, privacy needs, and whether the dashboard needs refresh automation.
Ministry and program dashboards should avoid standalone numbers when possible; compare measures to goals, historical baselines, or funnels so teams can interpret whether a result needs action.
Core Rock UI and UX work affects the components staff use daily, so developer guidance should consider usability and feedback loops, not just backend behavior.
Rock data quality work should be prioritized because dirty people, family, address, and duplicate data affects check-in, communication, reporting credibility, and leadership decisions.

Track recurring data defects in a shared backlog, choose a small set of fields or defect types to address first, set measurable cleanup goals, and share wins so ministry teams understand the operational value of clean Rock data.

This Data Analytics Hub walkthrough gives public-safe guidance for building a layered Rock reporting suite with Power BI or similar tools. It distinguishes executive, campus/ministry, and functional reporting, emphasizes comparison against goals or history, and shows when scheduled refreshes, live queries, Rock security roles, and embedded report pages each fit.
When BI reports are embedded back into Rock, teams still need to honor external licensing and put report pages behind appropriate Rock security roles.
